title: Uncountable nouns
subtitle: luggage, advice, information, weather
summary: Learn the everyday nouns that English treats as uncountable - no a/an and no plural - grouped by topic so that they are easier to remember.

lesson.heading: What are uncountable nouns?
lesson.text: Countable nouns can be used with **a/an** and made plural: *a hat, two hats*. Uncountable nouns are not normally used with a/an and have no plural. They are easiest to learn in groups associated with the same subject.

examples.text: Could you give me some **information**, please?
We bought some new **furniture** at the weekend.
I have some **news** for you: Henry is getting married.
examples.wrong: I have a news for you

lesson.heading: Groups of uncountable nouns
rows: luggage, baggage, accommodation, money, currency, information, transport, travel
food, sugar, rice, spaghetti, butter, bread, flour, soup
advice, knowledge, progress, research, work, homework, experience, wealth, poverty, happiness
cloth, silk, leather, coal, oil, stone, brick, plastic, equipment, software

lesson.heading: Abstract nouns in use
lesson.text: Many of the most useful abstract nouns in English are uncountable. Use **some**, **any**, **a lot of** or **a great deal of** with them instead of a number.

examples.text: She gave me some **advice** on how to study for the exam.
I picked up some interesting **knowledge** on that course.
She's made a lot of **progress** in a very short time.
She has done some **research** on marine life.
Do you have any **experience** of working with children?

left.label: travel (uncountable)
left.text: Use **travel** for the general idea of travelling.

right.label: a journey / a trip (countable)
right.text: For one individual occasion, use **journey** or **trip**.
examples: It was a very long **journey**. (not a very long travel)
She was away on a business **trip** for three days. (not a business travel)

lesson.heading: Uncountable and countable partners
lesson.note: Baggage is more common than luggage in American English.

lesson.heading: Verbs after uncountable nouns
lesson.text: An uncountable noun always takes a **singular** verb, even when it refers to a large amount. This catches out learners who translate directly from their own language.

examples.text: Her research **is** definitely making great progress these days.
examples.wrong: Her researches are making great progresses

examples.text: My knowledge in that area **is** very poor.
**Poverty** is the biggest problem in many countries.
examples.wrong: A poverty is the biggest problem

lesson.text: If you really need to count an uncountable noun, put a counting word in front of it: *a piece of advice*, *two items of luggage*, *a loaf of bread*.

exercises.prompt: Sort these nouns into uncountable and countable.
Match each uncountable noun with the countable noun that has a related meaning.
I'm sorry, I can't come. I have some ___ to do.
exercises.hint: (what the teacher gives you to do at home)
exercises.explanation: Homework is uncountable: some homework, not a homework or homeworks.

exercises.prompt: You'll need some ___ if you want to make a Chinese meal.
exercises.explanation: Rice, like sugar, flour and spaghetti, is uncountable.

exercises.prompt: I have some ___ for you: you're going to meet the President next week!
exercises.explanation: News looks plural but is uncountable and takes a singular verb: the news is good.

exercises.prompt: She's doing ___ teenage slang in English for her university project.
exercises.explanation: We do research into a subject; research is uncountable.

options: We had such terrible weather that we found some accommodation in town.
We had such a terrible weather that we found an accommodation in town.
We had such terrible weathers that we found accommodations in town.
We had such a terrible weather that we found some accommodations in town.
exercises.explanation: Weather and accommodation are both uncountable - no a/an, no plural.

exercises.prompt: In the south of England, most houses are made of ___, but in the north, ___ is more common.
exercises.explanation: As building materials, stone and brick are uncountable.

exercises.prompt: What ___ do you need to go skiing? If you can give me any ___, I would be grateful.
exercises.explanation: Equipment and information never take a plural -s.

exercises.statement: Oil exports have produced a great deal of wealth for the country.
exercises.explanation: Correct - wealth is uncountable and goes well with a great deal of.

exercises.statement: Package holidays often include transports from the airport to your accommodations.
exercises.explanation: Package holidays often include transport from the airport to your accommodation.

exercises.statement: I don't have any experiences of working in education, but I would like to do some voluntary works in a school.
exercises.explanation: I don't have any experience of working in education, but I would like to do some voluntary work in a school.

exercises.answer: I bought some new software that shows you the kind of weather every country has.
exercises.explanation: Software and weather are both uncountable, so neither takes a plural -s.
